title: What Is an Actuarial Salary? How to Convert Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay with Casual Loading and Super
description: Learn what an actuarial salary means, how to convert hourly pay to annual using 38 hours per week, and see how casual loading and super affect your total package.
salarySummary: For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, annual gross pay equals the hourly rate multiplied by 38 then by 52, with super paid on top.

faqs.q: What does 'actuarial salary' mean in the context of hourly pay?
faqs.a: An actuarial salary is the annualised figure you get by multiplying your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week and then by 52 weeks. It is a standard way to compare hourly wages with salaried offers, assuming a consistent 38-hour week and no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances.

faqs.q: How is casual loading applied when calculating my actuarial salary?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% paid on top of your base hourly rate to compensate for the lack of paid leave. Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading.

faqs.q: Does superannuation come out of my hourly rate or is it paid on top?

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding Your Actuarial Salary: From Hourly Rate to Annual Pay

When you are offered an hourly rate or a salary, it helps to see the full picture in annual terms. That is where the concept of an **actuarial salary** comes in. An actuarial salary is simply your hourly rate multiplied by the number of hours you work each week, then multiplied by 52 weeks. It gives you a standard annual figure you can use to compare job offers, budget, or check against award rates.

For a full-time employee in Australia, the standard working week is 38 hours. So the formula is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × 38 hours per week × 52 weeks**

If you work part-time or different hours, you can adjust the weekly hours accordingly. The calculator on [the timesheet](/) lets you enter your own hours. It also shows your fortnightly pay (weekly pay × 2), which is useful if you are paid every two weeks.

### The National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

From 1 July 2026, the national minimum wage set by the Fair Work Commission is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. This is the legal minimum for award/agreement-free adult employees. However, most workers are covered by an award or enterprise agreement that sets higher minimum rates. You can find the correct rate for your job using the [pay guides](/blog) from the Fair Work Ombudsman.

Award rates vary by industry and classification. They often include penalty rates for weekends, nights, or overtime, which are not factored into a simple actuarial salary calculation. The actuarial salary assumes the same rate every hour, so it is a baseline estimate.

### Casual Loading and Superannuation

Two important additions to your base hourly rate are casual loading and superannuation.

**Casual loading** is an extra 25% paid to casual employees to compensate for not receiving paid leave (annual leave, sick leave, etc.). The Fair Work Commission sets this at 25% on top of the minimum wage. For example, a casual employee on the national minimum wage would receive $33.05 per hour ($26.44 × 1.25). When you use the timesheet, check the casual loading box to add this automatically. Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading.

**Superannuation** is paid on top of your ordinary earnings. The super guarantee rate is 12% of your gross pay, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year (2026–27). Super is not deducted from your hourly rate or your actuarial salary; it is an additional contribution your employer must make. The calculator shows super as a separate amount.

### How to Use the Timesheet Calculator

On [the timesheet](/) (the home page), you type your base hourly rate. If you are a casual employee, tick the checkbox for 25% casual loading. The calculator then:

- Adds the loading to get your effective hourly rate
- Multiplies by your weekly hours (default 38)
- Multiplies by 52 to get annual gross pay
- Shows weekly, fortnightly, and annual figures
- Estimates super (12% on top) and tax (2026–27 resident rates with Medicare levy)

Remember: the annual figure is an estimate. It assumes you work the same hours every week with no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. For a more precise calculation, refer to your award or agreement.

### Tax and Take-Home Pay

Your actuarial salary is gross pay. To estimate your net (take-home) pay, the calculator applies the 2026–27 resident tax rates:

- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income over $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (with reductions for low-income earners). The calculator does not deduct HELP loans, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging. Visit the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page for more details.

### Important Considerations

An actuarial salary is a useful benchmark, but it is not a guarantee of your actual pay. Real-world factors such as:

- Unpaid overtime (common in salaried roles)
- Penalty rates (weekends, public holidays)
- Allowances (travel, tools, etc.)
- Salary packaging (e.g., novated leases)...can all change your effective hourly rate. Always check your award or enterprise agreement for the exact entitlements. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides free resources and a Pay and Conditions Tool.

For award/agreement-free employees, the national minimum wage applies. Casual employees get the 25% loading. Super is always on top.

### Summary

- **Actuarial salary** = hourly rate × weekly hours × 52
- Standard full-time hours: 38 per week
- Casual loading: 25% on top of base rate
- Super: 12% paid on top, up to $270,830
- Tax: 2026–27 resident rates + 2% Medicare
- Use [the timesheet](/) to calculate your figures

Whether you are comparing a casual job offer or checking your current salary, understanding your actuarial salary helps you make informed decisions.
